subject: english-literature
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the assessment objectives.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In poems exploring 'the effects of war', poets often present...
options: The physical and psychological suffering and lasting trauma of conflict
Only patriotic triumph with no complexity
questions.explain: War poetry frequently foregrounds suffering, trauma and the human cost rather than uncomplicated glory.

questions.q: The most analytical response to a striking image in an unseen poem is to...
options: Name the device, explore its effect, and link it to the poem's theme
State that the poet 'uses imagery' and move on
Skip it because it is unseen
questions.explain: Naming a method is only the start; exploring its effect and connecting it to meaning is what earns higher marks.

questions.q: How does a 'soliloquy' differ from an 'aside'?
options: An aside is always longer than a soliloquy
They are identical in every way
A soliloquy is delivered alone; an aside is a brief remark while others are on stage
An aside can only be spoken by the protagonist
questions.explain: An aside is a quick comment heard only by the audience while other characters remain on stage, whereas a soliloquy is spoken when the character is alone.

questions.q: In poems about 'nature', a common idea poets explore is...
options: Nature's power, beauty or indifference compared with human concerns
questions.explain: Nature poems often weigh human experience against nature's beauty, power or indifference to draw out a theme.

questions.q: A poem spoken in the voice of a single fictional speaker, revealing their character to a silent listener, is a...
questions.explain: A dramatic monologue uses one speaker's voice to expose their personality, often unintentionally, to an implied listener.

options: Contrasts with another to highlight that character's qualities
questions.explain: A foil's contrasting traits throw another character's qualities into sharper relief.

questions.q: A useful comparative connective to show contrast between two poems is...
questions.explain: Connectives like 'whereas', 'in contrast' and 'similarly' signal genuine comparison between the two poems' methods.

questions.q: When analysing an UNSEEN poem, the best first step is to...
options: Read for overall meaning and identify the main idea or feeling
questions.explain: Grasping the poem's central idea or feeling first gives you a framework to then analyse how methods create it.

options: The central character whose journey drives the narrative
The character who opposes the hero
questions.explain: The protagonist is the main character at the centre of the action, often in conflict with an antagonist.

questions.q: When a poem about 'loss' uses the present tense to describe a person now gone, the effect is often to...
options: Prove the poem is a sonnet
Keep the memory vivid and immediate, as if the person is still present
Confuse the reader for no reason
questions.explain: Present tense can make memory feel alive and ongoing, emphasising how loss keeps the absent person emotionally present.

questions.q: When poets present 'love and relationships', the tone may be...
options: Varied: tender, bitter, possessive or disillusioned depending on the poem
questions.explain: Relationship poems span many tones, so identifying the specific attitude to love is key to analysis.

questions.q: Repetition of a key word or phrase in a poem usually serves to...
options: Signal the end of the anthology
Emphasise an idea or emotion and create rhythm or insistence
questions.explain: Repetition foregrounds an idea, building emphasis, rhythm or a sense of obsession depending on context.
